title: Preparing for a Big Moment
author: Admired Leadership
summary: This article tackles a common but counterproductive instinct: treating a big opportunity as fundamentally different from ordinary work and therefore over-preparing for it. It argues that changing your process for a high-stakes moment actually raises anxiety and disrupts the rhythms that earned the opportunity in the first place. The piece draws on advice attributed to Peyton Manning about sticking to a consistent routine rather than reinventing one's approach under pressure. The core message is to treat the big moment as just another rep of the same preparation and execution that got you there, which paradoxically produces calmer, stronger performance.
points: Leaders often over-prepare for big moments by changing their usual process, which backfires.
New strategies designed only for the big moment leave less time to practice fundamentals.
Top performers treat the big moment like any other game, contest, or presentation.
Peyton Manning's advice was to keep the routine as close to normal as possible.
Framing the moment as ordinary helps the brain relax, settle in, and execute.
quotes: By preparing and planning differently for the big moment, leaders and performers magnify the pressure and stress that the fear of underperforming creates.
Designing new strategies and tactics designed just for the big moment leaves little time to practice and create the skills and repetition essential to high performance.
Avoid the distraction of new ideas and people. Stick with the fundamental planning and preparation that got you to the dance.
Keep your routine as close to the same as possible as you have all season.
The big moment shouldn't be anything more special than all the other moments that got you there.
